<reflection>
The first experiment provided initial kinetic data, but the fitting results show that many mechanisms have very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values, with differences often less than 0.5. This indicates that the moderate condition (S=1.0 M, cat=0.01 M, P=0.0) was not sufficiently discriminative. The top group includes mechanisms with simple catalytic cycles (M1, M7), deactivation (M9, M11), dimerization (M2), and others, all fitting nearly equally well. My aim for this turn is to propose an experiment that amplifies differences among these plausible mechanisms, particularly by probing catalyst concentration dependence, which is sensitive to dimerization, deactivation, and more complex pathways.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
I propose to increase the catalyst concentration to 0.05 M while keeping substrate at 1.0 M and product at 0.0 M. Higher catalyst concentration will stress pathways that depend on catalyst concentration, such as dimerization (M2, M3) and bimolecular deactivation (M13, M19). It may also alter the apparent reaction order in catalyst, helping distinguish simple Michaelis-Menten-like mechanisms (M1) from those with catalyst aggregation or deactivation. This condition avoids extreme saturation (substrate is still moderate) and avoids repeating the previous catalyst level. By moving to a higher catalyst regime, we expect to see differences in rate profiles, especially if deactivation or dimerization are present, without collapsing mechanistic distinctions. This design is effective because it targets multiple mechanistic classes simultaneously rather than just a single pair.
</hypothesis>
